blocks.text: Crop Fires, Weather Traps and Smog across Punjab: Data Preparation and Exploratory Analysis
Trans-Boundary Smog Prediction: Milestone 02, Draft Sections II and III, Merged Master Dataset
Munir Tariq (10067)  |  Ismail Nooruddin (09958)  |  Bilal Ayub (09716)  |  Data Science for Social Good, Habib University  |  October 2026
Abstract

Every winter, smoke from crop-residue burning and city emissions is trapped over the Punjab plain shared by Pakistan and India. This report describes how three independent data streams were cleaned and merged into one master dataset, and what the first analysis of that dataset shows. Hourly Open-Meteo air quality (CAMS model output), hourly Open-Meteo weather and 1.28 million NASA VIIRS fire detections were aligned to one UTC+5 clock and joined one-to-one into a table of 5,665 city-days (11 cities, 4 August 2022 to 31 December 2023) and 287 columns, with no missing predictor value. The target is a Composite Smog Index built from six standardised pollutants, with a city-specific spike label. On the training period, four results stand out. First, fires inside a ±45° upwind cone within 300 km track next-day smog (median Spearman ρ = 0.23 over the Pakistani cities in the harvest season), while a plain 300 km circle (−0.06) and a downwind placebo cone (0.01) do not. Second, the association is strongest one day after the fires. Third, stagnant and humid days roughly triple the next-day spike rate, and no rain day was followed by a spike. Fourth, spikes occur mainly in December and January, after the October–November burning peak, so fires alone do not make a spike: the weather must trap the smoke. Five formal hypotheses, mapped to columns of the master dataset, set up the modelling in Milestone 3.
1. Project Alignment and Master Dataset Overview

The project predicts hazardous smog spikes in Pakistani Punjab cities one to three days in advance from upwind crop-fire detections and from weather conditions that trap pollution. **Research question:** which fire and weather predictors, available on day *t*, explain Composite Smog Index spikes on days *t* + 1 to *t* + 3, and how much better than a persistence baseline and a weather-only baseline can they forecast those spikes? The work supports SDG 3 (targets 3.9 and 3.d: illness from air pollution and early warning), SDG 11 (target 11.6: urban air quality) and SDG 13 (regional climate action); the cross-border analysis also relates to SDG 17 (cooperation between countries). Following the instructor's feedback, the proposal's fixed target score (ROC-AUC above 0.88) has been dropped: the aim is to identify sound predictors and report the best honest performance.

blocks.text: 2. Data and Preprocessing (Draft Section II)
2.1 Collection audit

Each stream was collected and cleaned by one team member in its own notebook, then handed over as a clean daily table with its saved settings (Table 3). Air quality and weather were exported per city centre from Open-Meteo as hourly files in GMT. Both are gridded model estimates rather than station readings, so they suit comparisons between days and cities. Fire detections were downloaded from the NASA FIRMS archive as one file per country and year.

blocks.text: 2.2 Alignment, reshaping and merge

All raw times are in GMT. Each stream added 5 hours to the full timestamp **before** taking the calendar date, so that evening hours fall on the correct local day (26,626 fire detections moved to the next date). The same UTC+5 clock was used for the Indian cities so that all streams share day boundaries. The reshaping steps were: stacking the 11 city files of each stream (concat); aggregating hourly rows to one row per city-day (group-by with mean, maximum, total and vector-mean rules); building a long table of fire counts for every city, cone, radius and origin (602,250 rows) and pivoting the chosen settings into columns; and joining the three streams. City names come from one shared dictionary, so the keys are spelled identically in every table.

The merge started from an empty calendar of 11 cities × 515 days (5,665 rows), so that a missing day in any stream would remain visible. Air quality, weather and fire were then left-joined on city, country and date with a one-to-one check; the row count stayed at 5,665 after every join and every row found a partner. Lags of 1 to 3 days and the targets for days t+1 to t+3 were computed **within each city**, so that the last days of one city cannot leak into the first days of the next. Table 4 traces every row from the raw files to the master table.

blocks.text: 2.3 Missing data and selection bias

blocks.text: **Why no imputation.** The air-quality gap is not random: the source has no pollutant values before August 2022 in any city. Filling seven months by interpolation would invent the seasonal pattern the model must learn, so those rows were removed from every stream (listwise deletion of the block). In total 278 of the 287 master columns have no missing value.

**Selection bias.** (i) The training period contains only **one** harvest season (October–December 2022), so every seasonal estimate rests on one winter; the final test therefore retrains with the first half of 2024 and tests on the second half. (ii) On 13–16 December 2022 every pollutant is near zero in all cities at once, a likely source error. These 44 city-days are flagged (suspect_day = 1) and kept as rows: removing them would break each city's unbroken daily calendar, which the lags and targets rely on, and the flag lets Milestone 3 drop them in one step. They are already left out of the air-quality scaling and the spike thresholds. Their effect is reported: the index has a skewness of −1.15 on training days with them and +0.26 without them. (iii) The satellite cannot see fires under thick cloud or fog, which is common on the worst smog days, so fire–smog associations are likely underestimated. (iv) Islamabad and Rawalpindi share one air-quality series, so there are 10 independent air-quality series, not 11.
2.4 Transformations, scaling and the target
Variables with strong right skew were transformed with log(1 + x), which keeps zero values at zero (Table 6, Figure 1).

blocks.caption: **Table 6.** Skewness before and after log(1 + x), training period. Air-quality rows leave out the 44 flagged days, so they differ slightly from Table 9 (PM2.5 1.91, CO 3.17 with them).
rows: 10 of 13 air-quality columns had skew > 1 and were logged
61% of days have 0 mm, so the skew stays above 1
Fires in the upwind cone, 300 km

blocks.caption: **Figure 1.** Daily mean PM2.5 across the 11 cities on training days, (a) before and (b) after the log(1 + x) transform; dashed line = mean, solid line = median. The long right tail disappears after the transform. Produced by air_quality.ipynb (flagged December days left out).

blocks.text: **Standardisation.** Continuous predictors and pollutants were converted to z-scores, z = (x − mean)/SD, after the log transform where applied, using the mean and SD of the **training period only**. One set of parameters per variable is used for all cities, so real differences between cities remain, and the parameters are saved for reuse on 2024. Min-Max scaling was not used: a few extreme fire and rain days would squeeze almost every other day towards 0.

**Target.** Composite Smog Index = 0.40·z(PM2.5) + 0.12·[z(PM10) + z(NO2) + z(SO2) + z(O3) + z(CO)], computed from daily means. A **spike** is a day whose index is at or above the 90th percentile of that city's training October–March days. The thresholds run from 0.36 (Rahim Yar Khan) to 2.18 (Lahore) and give 297 spike city-days (5.2%) in the window.
2.5 Categorical encoding

Nominal variables were converted into 0/1 dummy columns, with one category dropped as the reference so that a regression with an intercept stays identifiable (Table 7). A numeric code (for example 0 to 7 for wind sectors) would impose a false order. The notebook confirms that every row belongs to exactly one category of each variable and that the eight wind-sector dummies are all 0 on exactly the 631 stagnant city-days. The workbook sheet Encoding_Example shows real rows next to their dummies.

blocks.text: 2.6 Spatial fire features

For each city, the great-circle distance and the compass bearing to every fire within 300 km were computed. A fire is **upwind** when its bearing lies within the cone half-angle (±30°, ±45° or ±60°) of the direction the daily wind comes from; a ±45° **downwind** cone is kept as a placebo. On stagnant days (daily vector-mean wind below 2 km/h, 10.9% of training city-days) the wind direction is unreliable, so the cone keeps every fire in the radius. Every count is split by origin (fires detected in India or in Pakistan), which makes the cross-border question testable (Figure 2). Automatic tests confirm that a north wind keeps fires to the north and that no cone holds more fires than its circle. The default setting, the ±45° upwind cone at 300 km, was chosen on the training harvest season only (Section 3.3).

blocks.text: 3. Exploratory Data Analysis (Draft Section III)

Unless stated otherwise, statistics use the 4,323 training city-days (1,012 in October–December 2022). The validation period is not analysed until Milestone 3, and 2024 is never used. All figures have a title, axes labelled with units, a legend where several series are shown, and a colour-blind-safe palette.
3.1 Univariate analysis

blocks.caption: **Table 9.** Summary statistics of the key variables, training period (n = 4,323 city-days).

blocks.text: **Resistant and non-resistant measures.** The weather variables are nearly symmetric (temperature range: mean 11.26 °C, median 11.30 °C, skew 0.02), so the mean and SD describe them well. The pollutants are moderately right-skewed (PM2.5 mean 54.4 µg/m³ against a median of 46.1 µg/m³). Fire counts and rain are zero-inflated and extremely skewed: fires in the cone have a mean of 43.3 but a median of 4, India-origin fires reach the cone on only 39% of days, and rain has a median of 0 mm against a mean of 2.2 mm. For these variables the median and IQR describe a typical day, while the mean describes the total load; the SD (4 to 51 times the IQR for the fire counts) is driven by a handful of days. Daily mean PM2.5 is above the WHO 24-hour guideline of 15 µg/m³ on 99.4% of training city-days outside the flagged days; as these are model estimates, this is an indication rather than an official exceedance count.
3.2 Outlier diagnostic

blocks.caption: **Table 10.** Outliers by the z-score rule (|z| > 3) and the quartile rule (beyond Q1 − 1.5·IQR or Q3 + 1.5·IQR), training period. Masked = extra points the z-rule finds once the first-pass z-outliers are removed. SD inflation = SD of all days relative to the SD without the IQR outliers.

blocks.text: **Masking.** The quartile rule flags far more days than the z-rule in every skewed variable (rain 823 against 89; fires in the cone 534 against 63; PM2.5 292 against 96). Extreme days inflate the SD, which widens the 3-SD limit and hides other extreme days: removing the first-pass z-outliers and applying the rule again finds 144 more rain days, 101 more fire days and 63 more PM2.5 days. **Variance inflation.** Without the quartile-rule outliers, the SD of rain falls from 6.26 to 0.43 mm and that of fires in the cone from 177 to 14.6, so for zero-inflated variables the SD consists mostly of the outliers. On the log scale, fires in the cone have no quartile-rule outliers at all. **Decision.** No outlier was deleted, capped or winsorised: they are real smog episodes, storms and fire outbreaks, the events the project predicts. Each stream carries 0/1 flag columns instead.
3.3 Bivariate and multivariate analysis

**When do spikes happen?** Table 11 groups the training days by season, wind, rain and country. By month, spikes are concentrated in **December (26.1% of city-days) and January (22.9%)**, against 2.3% in October and 4.2% in November, while fires in the cone peak in October and November (57,087 and 50,062 detections). The wheat-burning season of May 2023 (30,235 cone detections) produced **no** spike. Fires alone therefore do not make a spike: the smoke must be trapped by winter weather (Figure 3).

blocks.caption: **Table 11.** Mean Composite Smog Index and share of spike days by group, training period.

**Figure 3.** Composite Smog Index over time (7-day centred average; no unit, 0 = average training day) for Lahore, Faisalabad, Rahim Yar Khan and Amritsar, 4 August 2022 to 31 December 2023. Grey bands mark October–December; dashed and dotted lines mark the end of training and the start of validation. The break in December 2022 is the flagged suspect days. Produced by air_quality.ipynb.

blocks.text: **Contingency tables.** On the training harvest days, 27.3% of days after a stagnant day were spikes, against 9.4% after a ventilated day (χ² = 24.4, odds ratio 3.61, 95% CI 2.15–6.06). After a day with at least one fire in the cone, 12.0% of next days were spikes, against 2.6% after a day with none (χ² = 8.3, odds ratio 5.11, 95% CI 1.60–16.37). Consecutive days of a city are not independent, so these p-values (< 0.01) overstate certainty and the tables describe association only.

blocks.caption: **Figure 4.** Spearman rank correlations between the next-day Composite Smog Index, today's index, fire counts (±45° upwind cone at 300 km, by origin, and the plain 300 km circle) and daily weather, 1,012 training harvest city-days. Temperature range = daily max − min (°C); rain = daily total (mm); vector-mean wind = length of the averaged wind vector (km/h). Diverging scale centred on 0. Produced by merge_analysis.ipynb.

blocks.text: **Correlations (Figure 4).** Today's index is by far the strongest correlate of tomorrow's (ρ = 0.82), which makes persistence the baseline every model must beat. Among the predictors, wind speed (−0.38), fires in the upwind cone (0.34), humidity (0.32), vector-mean wind (−0.31), temperature range (0.30) and rain (−0.29) relate to the next-day index, while the plain 300 km circle is weaker (0.19). Wind speed and vector-mean wind are nearly redundant (0.85), as are mean, minimum and maximum temperature (r = 0.91–0.98), so models will use one of each pair.

**Fire cone and radius (Figure 5).** In the harvest season the cone matters more than the circle. At 300 km the ±45° upwind cone gives a median ρ of 0.23 (positive in all 7 Pakistani cities), the plain circle -0.06 and the downwind placebo 0.01: a large circle counts as many fires downwind as upwind and so carries no signal. Inside the cone, ρ grows with the radius, so the smoke that matters is regional. The ±30° and ±60° cones give similar values; with 92 days per city a correlation has a standard error of about 0.10, so ±45° was kept as the middle setting. Over the full training year every 300 km setting looks good (0.16–0.35), **including the placebo**, because fires and smog share a seasonal cycle; this is why the selection used the harvest season only. The cone count is most related to smog **one day later** (median ρ = 0.24, against 0.16 on the same day, 0.11 after two days and 0.05 after three; the window here is set on the smog day, hence the small difference from 0.23). At the median vector-mean wind of about 5 km/h, smoke travels roughly 120 km a day, consistent with a one-to-two-day delay.

blocks.caption: **Figure 5.** Median Spearman correlation between the fire count on day t and the Composite Smog Index on day t + 1, for every cone and radius, computed within each city. Top: training harvest season (92 days per city), used to choose the setting (black box). Bottom: full training year (393 days per city), where the shared seasonal cycle inflates every setting, including the placebo. Near border = Lahore, Sialkot; Far = Multan, Rahim Yar Khan, Islamabad, Rawalpindi. Produced by merge_analysis.ipynb.

blocks.text: **Weather traps (Figure 6).** Stagnant days are followed by a spike 27.3% of the time (9.4% otherwise) and humid days 22.0% (8.5%). No rain day was followed by a spike (0 of 72). When stagnation, no rain and high humidity coincide, 45% of next days are spikes (9 of 20, risk ratio 4.4). The temperature-range proxy points the other way from the work plan: none of the 61 small-range days was followed by a spike, while large-range days (> 13.6 °C) were followed by 15.4% (risk ratio 1.77). A small day–night range signals cloud or rain, which mix and wash the air, whereas surface inversions form on clear, calm nights with strong cooling, so a **large** range is used as the inversion proxy.

blocks.caption: **Figure 6.** Share of next days that are smog spikes when today has each weather condition (filled circles, 95% Wilson intervals) and on all other days (hollow diamonds), training harvest season. Dashed line: rate over all harvest days (11.0%); n = city-days with the condition. Produced by merge_analysis.ipynb.

blocks.text: **Cross-border check.** Only Lahore (54 days with India-origin fires in the cone), Sialkot (45) and Faisalabad (40) receive India-origin fires often enough to test the cross-border claim; in Multan, Rahim Yar Khan, Islamabad and Rawalpindi this happens on 1 to 18 days only. In Sialkot, India-origin fires go with higher next-day smog (ρ = 0.33, against 0.10 for Pakistan-origin fires); in Lahore it is the other way round (-0.04 against 0.23), although 70% of the fires in Lahore's cone are Indian. The cross-border signal is therefore mixed and rests on one season; hypothesis H4 tests it with controls.

**Robustness of the index weights.** Rebuilding the index with equal weights, without ozone or without PM10 ranks the days almost identically (Spearman ρ ≥ 0.979). Dropping ozone changes the most spike labels (68 city-days, against 208 training spikes in the main index), because winter ozone moves opposite to NO2. The main weights are kept and the ozone sensitivity is listed as a limitation.
4. Hypotheses and Analytical Plan

Each hypothesis starts from a pattern in Section 3 and is mapped to columns of the master dataset (Table 12). The response is always measured on day t + 1 (t + 1 to t + 3 for H5) and uses only information known on day t. The full mapping, with the planned test for each hypothesis, is in the workbook sheet Hypothesis_Mapping.

blocks.text: **Analytical plan.** Consecutive days of a city are correlated, and Islamabad and Rawalpindi share air-quality values, so H1–H4 use regressions with city-clustered standard errors or a block bootstrap: logistic regression for the spike label and linear regression for the index, with interaction terms for H3 and H4. Non-linear effects will be checked with gradient-boosted trees and permutation importance. For H5, models are compared on the validation season (1,309 city-days, 1,012 of them in October–December 2023) against persistence (persist_index, persist_spike) and a weather-only model. Because spikes are rare (5.2%), results are reported as PR-AUC, recall and precision as well as ROC-AUC and the Brier score, and as MAE for the index. Because the spike label falls mainly in December–January, after the burning peak, Milestone 3 will also report results for the continuous index and compare a label with month-specific thresholds.
5. Limitations

items: **Model-based air quality.** Open-Meteo air quality is CAMS model output on a coarse grid, not monitor data; neighbouring cities can share values (Islamabad = Rawalpindi).
**One training winter.** Every learned threshold, scaling parameter and the cone choice rest on one harvest season (92 days per city); differences in ρ of about 0.1 are within noise.
**No pressure and no direct inversion measure.** Surface pressure was not in the exported files; temperature range and stagnation are proxies.
**Satellite fire detection.** VIIRS misses fires under thick cloud or fog and between its overpasses; counts are detections, not fires.
**Simplifications.** Each city is one point, the cone uses one daily wind direction, one UTC+5 clock is used for India (IST is UTC+5:30), and observed weather stands in for forecast weather.
**Dependence.** City-days are not independent (multi-day episodes, shared regional weather), so group comparisons and contingency p-values are descriptive.

blocks.text: 6. Reproducibility and Deliverables

The notebooks air_quality.ipynb (A), weather.ipynb (B), fire.ipynb (C) and merge_analysis.ipynb (Role 2) run top to bottom with Restart and Run All, in this order, from the project root, and keep all their printed outputs and figures. They share one settings file (src/config.py: cities, coordinates, dates, file names) and helper modules for the merge, the EDA and one figure style. Every setting is learned on the training period and saved, so the final run on 2024 only changes the dates in the settings file. The last cell of merge_analysis.ipynb writes the workbook Milestone2_Final_Master_and_EDA.xlsx: its first sheet is the master table (5,665 × 287), and its Contents sheet lists the other sheets (data dictionary, missing values for every column, decisions log, saved parameters, encoding example, the final table of each stream, and every EDA table of this report) together with the table or figure that uses each one.
